runtime_boundary: Represents the tensorflow_model_server binary and the serving libraries in the tensorflow/serving repository, not the TensorFlow framework in tensorflow/tensorflow. The framework builds and trains models and supplies the session runtime this server links against; the server's own documentation states that it deals with the inference aspect of machine learning, taking models after training and managing their lifetimes, which is the separate product this record reviews. TensorFlow Lite and LiteRT are a different execution stack for mobile and embedded targets and are out of scope here; the server carries only an experimental --prefer_tflite_model flag that picks up a model.tflite file inside a SavedModel directory, which the flag text marks as removable at any time. Managed Google Cloud offerings that host this server for customers, including Vertex AI prebuilt TensorFlow prediction containers, hold the serving contract themselves and are inference-service boundaries rather than part of this record. The server is headless, operated as a container, an APT-installed binary, or a Kubernetes deployment, and ships no graphical or conversational interface, which keeps it on the runtime side of the ADR 015 runtime-versus-assistant test.
model_management: Models are staged by the operator as numbered version directories under a model_base_path; there is no fetch, pull, registry, or removal command. The server polls the filesystem on --file_system_poll_wait_seconds and loads new versions automatically. A ModelServerConfig file names multiple models and sets a model_version_policy of latest, specific versions, or all, and version_labels attach names such as stable and canary that clients address through the request ModelSpec or a /v1/models/<name>/labels/<label> REST path. The config is reloaded either by polling --model_config_file_poll_wait_seconds or through a HandleReloadConfigRequest RPC, and the server realizes only the new config, so a model absent from it is unloaded. Version policies are Availability Preserving or Resource Preserving, load and unload run on sized thread pools with retry settings, and SavedModel warmup replays PredictionLogs from assets.extra at load time. There is no adapter or LoRA mechanism; custom model types enter through C++ Source, SourceAdapter, and Loader extension points.
hardware_requirements: Documented execution is CPU and NVIDIA GPU on Linux. The APT channel publishes tensorflow-model-server, built with platform-specific SSE4 and AVX instructions, and tensorflow-model-server-universal for machines without them; the documentation states that only Linux binaries are supported when building from source. GPU serving uses the tensorflow/serving:latest-gpu image, current NVIDIA drivers, and nvidia-docker or docker --gpus. There is no documented ROCm, Metal, Vulkan, NPU, or DirectML path, and no documented multi-GPU or multi-host model-parallel serving; scale beyond one process is by replicas. The binary carries a --skip_initialize_tpu flag and experimental --xla_cpu_compilation_enabled, --xla_gpu_compilation_enabled, and --mixed_precision=bfloat16 flags whose behaviour is described in the source rather than in the published guides.
operational_controls: Batching is off by default and enabled with --enable_batching plus a BatchingParameters file setting max_batch_size, batch_timeout_micros, num_batch_threads, max_enqueued_batches, and optional allowed_batch_sizes; scheduling is global across all models and versions on the server unless --enable_per_model_batching_parameters is set. Concurrency and resource limits cover rest_api_num_threads, rest_api_timeout_in_ms, grpc_max_threads, tensorflow_session_parallelism with intra- and inter-op settings, a thread_pool_factory_config_file, and per_process_gpu_memory_fraction. Transport security is configured through an SSLConfig file for the gRPC channel and optional Google ALTS credentials; the REST surface has no documented TLS or authentication and offers only CORS headers, so public exposure depends on a proxy. Observability is a MonitoringConfig that enables a Prometheus endpoint at a configured path collecting both serving and core TensorFlow metrics, a model status API on REST and gRPC, an optional standard gRPC health-check service, sampled request logging, and a profiler service consumed through TensorBoard.
strengths: Version handling is the most developed in the collection: numbered version directories, latest, specific, and all version policies, string version labels for canary and rollback addressable from both APIs, availability- or resource-preserving load ordering, and config reload by polling or RPC without restarting the server.
The request batching scheduler is separately documented and tunable, schedules globally across every loaded model and version, and can be limited to a fixed set of allowed batch sizes.
The gRPC PredictionService and ModelService protos and their mirrored REST endpoints are stable, versioned, and specific enough that other servers reimplement them as a compatibility surface.

Operational surfaces are complete for a classic server: Prometheus metrics, model status and metadata endpoints, a gRPC health check, sampled request logging, a TensorBoard profiler, container and APT install paths with a documented upgrade command, and a Kubernetes deployment guide.
tradeoffs: Accelerator coverage is CPU and NVIDIA GPU on Linux only, with no support matrix published and no ROCm, Metal, Vulkan, or NPU path.

The server executes TensorFlow SavedModel graphs and nothing else; there is no conversion tooling of its own, no quantization scheme it applies, and the only other loadable artifact is a model.tflite file behind a flag the source marks as experimental and removable.

The API is deliberately tensor-shaped: predict, classify, regress, and multi-inference with no streaming, no embeddings endpoint, no tool calling, and no structured output, and no OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible surface, so LLM clients cannot address it without an adapter.
There is no KV-cache management and no distributed or multi-host serving; a large model must fit the process, and scale is by replicas.

REST has no documented authentication or transport security, and several published pages are dated: the documentation site renders under TensorFlow v2.16.1 while releases have reached 2.20.0, GPU instructions still reference nvidia-docker, and the flag reference defers to main.cc for anything beyond a short list.
license_note: The repository publishes a single Apache-2.0 license file at the root, with the appendix completed as 'Copyright 2016, The TensorFlow Serving Authors.'; the AUTHORS file names Google Inc. as the copyright holder. A recursive listing of the default branch shows no NOTICE, COPYING, or additional per-directory license file. The third_party directory holds only Bazel BUILD files and patches for boost, darts_clone, icu, libevent, rapidjson, sentencepiece, tensorflow, tf_decision_forests, and tf_text, whose own terms govern those upstream sources and do not alter the project's Apache-2.0 grant. GitHub's detected SPDX value of Apache-2.0 agrees with the file text, which was read in full rather than inferred from the badge.
